t: Topic, aim and lesson plan
n: In this lesson we shall first consider sawing wounds, then transport trauma and its types: car, motorcycle, rail, tractor and aviation trauma. According to the World Health Organization, more than 1.2 million people die in road traffic accidents every year, and more than 50 million are injured. According to forensic medical examination data, transport trauma accounts for 60-65% of deaths from mechanical injuries. The aim of the lesson is to understand the mechanism of injury formation and to learn to give recommendations for the prevention of traumatism on the basis of examination materials.

t: Sawing wounds: signs depending on the type of saw
n: In sawing wounds, the signs differ depending on the type of saw. The general rule is this: the kerf is wider than the thickness of the saw blade. Small particles of soft tissue and bone sawdust are found inside the wound and at its edges. Now let us compare the types. When the saw is struck, many small stab wounds form, and with a strong blow, tissue bridges remain at the bottom. With a circular saw, the wound edges are uneven and serrated, the bone surface is smooth, and the mark is arc-shaped. With a hand saw, the edge is linear and finely serrated, and the bone shows parallel ridges and grooves. Remember: with a circular saw the mark is arc-shaped, with a hand saw it is parallel.

t: The concept of transport trauma and the history of its separation
n: Now the concept of transport trauma. Transport trauma is the totality of injuries received from the external and internal parts of moving vehicles and in falls from them. Its types: car, motorcycle, bicycle, tractor, rail, aviation and water transport trauma. If different vehicles collide, this is called combined transport trauma. Because of the frequency of cases and the peculiarities of the injury mechanism and of the examination, transport trauma has been set apart as a separate section since the 1960s. In the examination of living persons, transport trauma accounts for 20-25% of mechanical injuries.

t: Transport trauma: statistical indicators
n: Let us turn to the statistical indicators. According to the World Health Organization, more than 1.2 million people die in road traffic accidents each year. In these accidents more than 50 million people suffer bodily injuries of varying severity. According to World Bank estimates, material damage amounts to 1.5-2.0% of the gross domestic product, that is, GDP, of all countries. According to examination data, the share in deaths is 60-65%, in living persons 20-25%, and the share of car trauma is more than 90%. It is important not to confuse these figures.

t: Types of transport trauma
n: Transport trauma is the totality of injuries received from parts of moving transport or in a fall from it. Its types: car, motorcycle, bicycle, tractor, rail, aviation and water transport trauma. Since the 1960s transport trauma has been set apart as a separate section of forensic medicine. The trauma may be simple or combined. In simple trauma, one type of vehicle is involved. In combined trauma, different vehicles collide, for example a motorcycle with a car or a car with a tractor.

t: Quick question 1: basics of transport trauma
n: The first quick question: what is transport trauma? Answer: the totality of injuries received from parts of a moving vehicle and in a fall from it. Second question: what share of examinations is accounted for by car trauma? Answer: more than 90%. Third question: what is combined transport trauma? Answer: injury received in a collision of vehicles of different kinds. Attention, there is a risk of error: in deaths the share is 60-65%, in living persons 20-25%. Do not confuse these two indicators.

t: Procedure for preserving clothing and footwear
n: The procedure for preserving clothing and footwear. The physician fully examines and describes the injury and also pays attention to the victim's clothing and footwear. The reason is that clothing and footwear may bear traces of injury and contamination that are important for investigating the incident. The work is therefore done in sequence: first the clothing is removed carefully, then dried under room conditions, then placed in paper packaging and handed to the staff of the authority. Analysis of examination materials, in turn, supplies proposals and recommendations in developing measures to reduce traumatism.

t: Classification of car trauma: six types
n: Classification of car trauma. According to the classification of Matyshev and co-authors, 1968, six types of car trauma are distinguished. The first and second types: collision and being run over by a wheel. The third and fourth types: injury inside the cabin and falling out of the car. The fifth and sixth types: compression and combined trauma, that is, of two or several kinds. Each type occurs in different variants, and the injuries are inseparably linked not only to the type but also to the variant. Injuries arise through the mechanisms of blow, compression, tension, friction and concussion.

t: Four groups of injuries in car trauma
n: In car trauma, injuries are divided into four groups by diagnostic significance, which helps to establish the mechanism of injury. The first is the specific injury: it corresponds to the shape and size of a part, for example the mark of a headlamp or tyre tread. The second is the characteristic injury: it corresponds to the type or phase of car trauma, for example a bumper injury or a whiplash fracture. The third is the non-characteristic injury: an abrasion or bruise, from which the type cannot be judged. The fourth is the imitation injury, which resembles an injury from another incident. Attention: a characteristic injury and a non-characteristic injury are not the same thing.

t: Specific and characteristic injuries
n: A specific injury is produced by the action of a particular part of the car, that is, a headlamp, front trim or tyre tread. It is therefore also called a contact injury. Its shape, size and pattern correspond to the part that was in contact. From it the type of car trauma, and sometimes the particular car, can be established. A characteristic injury corresponds to a certain type or phase of car trauma. Examples: bumper injury, traces of sliding and dragging, multiple rib fractures. Other characteristic injuries: bloody "pockets" in soft tissue, a "whiplash" fracture of the cervical vertebrae, and multiple fractures of the sternum and pelvic bones.

t: Non-characteristic and imitation injuries
n: A non-characteristic injury has neither specific nor characteristic features. Therefore no precise conclusion about car trauma can be drawn from it. This group includes mainly abrasions, bruises and some wounds on the victim's body. An imitation injury, by contrast, resembles injuries from other incidents. For example, fragments of the windscreen resemble a cut or stab-cut wound. Attention: an injury from bolts protruding outwards resembles a stab wound. Therefore do not draw hasty conclusions from the shape of the wound alone.

t: Case analysis: determining the injury group
n: Case analysis. Situation: in car trauma, the victim's body shows only abrasions and bruises. No shape resembling the mark of a headlamp, bumper or tyre has been found. First question: which of the four groups do these injuries belong to, and can a precise conclusion about car trauma be drawn from them? Addition to the situation: a cut wound resembling windscreen fragments has been found on the face. Second question: which group does this wound belong to? Direction of the answer: abrasions and bruises belong to the non-characteristic group, and a cut wound from glass fragments to the imitation group. Injuries of both these groups do not on their own prove car trauma.

t: Collision with a pedestrian: four phases
n: A collision of a pedestrian with a moving car is the most common type of car trauma. It consists of four phases. First phase: impact by parts of the car. Second phase: falling onto the car. Third phase: being thrown and falling to the ground. Fourth phase: sliding along the ground. But not all four phases are always present. In a strike by a lorry, a van-bodied vehicle or the side of a car, the second phase is not observed. In young children the second phase is also absent. At low speed the fourth phase may be absent.

t: Bumper injuries and their significance
n: Bumper injuries and their significance. Bone injury depends on the height of the bumper and the speed of movement at the moment of impact. A transverse abrasion, bruise or wound appears on the skin. In a strike by a passenger car, the bones of the lower leg break, and in a strike by a lorry, the bones of the thigh. The shape of the fracture is triangular, with the base on the side of the impact. If the bumper is thin and the speed exceeds 55-60 km/h, there may be an annular fracture in the bone. From a bumper injury one judges the make, speed, region of primary impact and position of the victim.

t: Injuries by phases of the collision
n: Let us consider injuries by phases of the collision. In the first phase, in the area of primary action, there may be contact abrasions and bruises in the shape of a headlamp, lower lamp or front trim. In the second phase, mainly on the head and chest, there are abrasions, bruises, wounds, bone fractures and internal organ injuries; they lie on the side of the first impact. In the third phase, on the side opposite the first impact, external and internal injuries arise in all regions from the blow against the ground and concussion. In the fourth phase, parallel abrasions form, corresponding to the direction of sliding.

t: Quick question 2: collision with a pedestrian
n: The second quick question. How many phases are there in a collision with the front of the vehicle? Answer: four: impact, falling onto the car, being thrown and falling to the ground, sliding along the ground. What does a bumper injury look like? Answer: a transverse abrasion, bruise or wound. A bumper fracture is triangular, with its base on the side of the primary impact. Which bones break? The bones of the lower leg with a passenger car, and the bones of the thigh with a lorry. Attention: with a lorry, a van-bodied vehicle, a side strike, and in young children, there is no second phase. Sliding marks are parallel abrasions.

t: Being run over by a wheel: types and phases
n: Being run over by a wheel is divided into types and phases. In a complete run-over, the wheel passes across the body; in an incomplete one, it only rides onto the body. The direction relative to the axis of the body may be transverse, oblique or longitudinal. The process consists of five phases. First: the wheel strikes the body. Second: the body is displaced in the direction of travel. Third: the wheel rides onto the body. Fourth: the wheel comes off the body. Fifth: secondary displacement. The main severe injury arises from compression of the body between the wheel and the ground.

t: Marks of the wheel tyre tread
n: Marks of the wheel tyre tread are of two kinds: an injury mark, that is, a bruise and abrasion, or a superimposed mark, that is, contamination. Among specific injuries, tyre tread imprints are relatively common in practice. On the skin, the raised part of the tread leaves a positive mark: abrasion and bruise. The recessed part leaves a negative mark: a bruise only. On clothing, tread marks occur mainly as a superimposed mark, that is, as contamination. Thus an injury mark is found on the skin, and a superimposed mark on clothing.

t: Injuries by body region in a run-over
n: In a run-over, injuries differ by region of the body. When a wheel passes over the head, there are multiple fractures of the skull and facial bones, crushing of the brain, and the auricle may be wholly or partly detached. When it passes over the chest, the ribs break along many lines on both sides; if the victim is lying on the back, the scapulae and spinous processes of the vertebrae also break. In the abdominal region the internal organs are injured and displaced. In the pelvis the bones break in many places, and in the legs there are comminuted fractures. Injury is more severe on the side where the wheel came off the body. At a speed of 20 km/h and above, the wheel "jumps off" the body, and there may be no injury in the 4th phase.

t: Case analysis: wheel mark
n: Case analysis: wheel mark. Situation: a wheel tyre tread mark has been found on the victim's trousers, and strip-like abrasions parallel to the direction of travel on the body. Recall: a tread mark on clothing is mainly a superimposed mark, that is, contamination. On the body the raised part leaves a positive mark and the recessed part a negative one. On one side, "pockets" filled with blood have been found under the skin, and on the opposite side, skin tears. This shows the side from which the wheel came off the body. Question: from which side did the wheel come off? In which phases do strip-like abrasions form, and why are the marks important?

t: Inside the car: driver's injuries
n: Let us consider the driver's injuries inside the car. On striking the steering wheel, a semilunar abrasion and bruise appear on the chest, and fractures of the sternum and ribs are possible. Injuries are located on the front and left surfaces of the body; fractures of the femur and tibia are more often on the left. A print of the pedals remains on the sole of the footwear. At high speed an annular fracture of the occipital bone is possible. In the driver the process runs in four phases: the feet strike the panel, the chest strikes the steering wheel, the head strikes the windscreen, then the body and neck are thrown backwards.

t: Passenger injuries and the seat belt
n: Passenger injuries and the seat belt. The body of a front-seat passenger is not restrained. For this reason this position is recognised as the most dangerous in the cabin; fractures of the skull and face and injuries of the internal organs occur here. Rear-seat passengers have fewer injuries, which arise mainly from striking the back of the front seat. The belt prevents injury. But if the speed exceeds the set limit, the belt itself becomes an injuring factor: the ligaments of the neck, the sternum and the clavicle are injured. At high speed a passenger may be thrown out through the windscreen.

t: Falling out of a car: three phases
n: Falling out of a car consists of three phases. In the first phase, from striking parts of the car, abrasions and bruises, and sometimes contused and lacerated wounds, appear. The main injuries form in the second phase, on landing on the ground. They are direct and indirect and depend on the part of the body that landed on the ground. In the third phase the body slides and parallel strip-like abrasions appear. It is precisely these abrasions that help to distinguish this injury from a fall from a height.

t: Compression and the particulars of examination questions
n: In compression there are two phases: first an impact with the outer parts of the car, then compression of the body between the car and another object. In the second phase there are multiple fractures of the chest wall and pelvic bones, and the internal organs of the thoracic, abdominal and pelvic cavities are injured. The body may show an ecchymotic outline of clothing, that is, a mark of seams and folds in the form of haemorrhage into the skin. If the chest and abdomen are compressed, death from compression asphyxia is possible. In the examination, besides the usual tasks, the type of car trauma, the make, the mechanism, the victim's position, the acting part and direction, and sometimes the speed are determined.

t: Case analysis: injury inside the cabin
n: Case analysis: injury inside the cabin. Situation: a car struck a stationary object; the driver and the front-seat passenger were injured. Question: whose injuries are more severe, and why? In the driver, the injuries are on the front and left surfaces of the body; from striking the steering wheel a semilunar abrasion and bruise appear on the chest. The body of the front-seat passenger is not restrained, so the injury is more serious than the driver's; this position is considered the most dangerous in the cabin. Attention, there is a risk of error: in the driver the abrasions are from parts of the left door, in the passenger from projections of the right door. On the passenger's face, multiple abrasions and cut wounds from windscreen fragments are found.

t: Quick question 3: wheel and cabin trauma
n: The third quick question: wheel and cabin trauma. First question: how many phases are there in being run over by a wheel? Answer: five. The first is the wheel striking the body, and the last is the secondary displacement of the body behind the wheel. Second question: what marks do the raised and recessed parts of the tread leave? Answer: the raised part leaves a positive mark, that is, abrasion and bruise; the recessed part a negative mark, that is, bruise only.

t: Quick question 3: wheel and cabin trauma (continued)
n: The quick question continued. Which seat is the most dangerous in the cabin? Answer: the front seat. Rear-seat passengers are injured relatively less. Second question: why may there be no injury in the fourth phase? Answer: at a speed of 20 km/h and above, the wheel "jumps off" the body.

t: Motorcycle trauma
n: Motorcycle trauma is much rarer than car trauma and is observed mainly in late spring, summer and early autumn. A motorcycle is unstable, so the driver and passenger may be injured in any position. Characteristic injury: a strip-like abrasion, contused wound and fracture of the fibula on the anteromedial surface of the lower leg and thigh. There are five types of motorcycle trauma: collision with a pedestrian, being run over by a wheel, falling off the motorcycle, collision with another object, and combined trauma.

t: Motorcycle trauma: mechanism of injury
n: Mechanism of injury in motorcycle trauma. When a motorcycle collides with a pedestrian, the blow is delivered by the wheel, the fitting above it, the handlebar, the lever and the footboard; the 4th phase, that is, displacement along the ground, is not observed. In the area of the legs, pelvis and abdomen there are abrasions, bruises and contused-lacerated wounds; in some cases the bones of the lower leg, thigh and pelvis break. In the driver and passenger, a strip-like abrasion on the anteromedial surface of the lower leg and thigh, a contused wound and a fracture of the fibula are characteristic. In a passenger in a sidecar, the ankle and knee joints are injured. From the handlebar lever, there is an abrasion on the palm between the 1st and 2nd fingers.

t: Rail trauma: types and specific features
n: Rail trauma is the totality of injuries received from a locomotive, electric locomotive and carriages; the tram is included here. It has six types: collision, being run over by a wheel, falling from a carriage, injury inside the vehicle, compression and combined rail trauma. In a fall from the roof of a carriage the injuries are more severe than in a fall from a car, because the speed and height are greater. Traces of oil, ballast and coal particles on clothing and body are often considered characteristic of rail trauma.

t: Rails: pressure bands and sliding bands
n: In rail trauma there are pressure bands and sliding bands. On compressed skin, a T-shaped abrasion forms from friction; it is called the "pinch" sign and is found at the place where the wheel left. The pressure band is at first soft and whitish; on drying it becomes coarse and dark brown; on the wheel side its width is 12-14 cm, and on the rail side 7-8 cm. In the sliding band, arc-shaped deep scratches and signs of contamination are found; at the edge it is 2-15 cm and wider on the wheel side. With a light carriage, a mark of 2-4 cm is seen on the skin and 12-14 cm in width beneath the skin.

t: Rails: division of the body and bone fractures
n: Division of the body and bone fractures in rail trauma. The body is compressed between the wheel and the rail with a force of 5 tonnes or more per sq. cm and is crushed. The wheel flange acts like scissors and divides the tissues, and the body is dismembered. On the rail side the edges of the division are relatively smooth. On the wheel side the skin flaps are coarsely toothed, and their corners point in the direction of travel of the vehicle. The edge of a long tubular bone fracture outside the rail is smooth, and between the rails it is curved; between them are small bone fragments.

t: Rails: division of the body and bone fractures (continued)
n: Continued. Because the tissues are crushed and squeezed outwards, a wedge-shaped defect forms. If the fragments are brought together, the rail side matches, while on the wheel side a gap remains.

t: Tractor trauma
n: Tractor trauma is rare and is observed mainly in rural areas; the injury depends on the construction of the tractor. The teeth of the track catch clothing and body and draw them under the tractor; the action of the teeth is very great. In compression the external injury is not marked, the internal organs are severely injured, and death from asphyxia is possible. With a wheeled tractor, the 2nd phase is not observed in a collision; in a run-over the mass and wheel size are taken into account, and the tread mark differs from that of a car. With a tracked tractor, there is no 4th phase in a collision and no 2nd phase in a run-over, and a mark corresponding to the track links remains on clothing.

t: Aviation trauma: types and injuring factors
n: Aviation trauma is the totality of injuries to crew, passengers and other persons connected with an aircraft. It has four types: inside the aircraft during flight, on leaving the aircraft in flight, on impact with the ground, and injury by the aircraft on the ground. The factors: dynamic and impact overload, oncoming airflow, explosion and altitude decompression. In flight above 8 km, if pressurisation fails, explosive decompression occurs; above 19 km, altitude emphysema appears.

t: Aviation trauma: injuring factors
n: In aviation trauma there are eight injuring factors: dynamic and impact overload, airflow, two kinds of decompression, cabin objects, blast wave, thermal factor and external parts. In dynamic overload, anaemia or plethora of the brain, fainting and visual disturbance are observed. Impact overload, for example in ejection or a hard landing, produces compression fractures of the skull, limb bones and spine. Airflow at a speed of 800 km/h and above acts like a solid body.

t: Pilot's injuries: cabin and harness marks
n: Pilot's injuries: cabin and harness marks. In a collision or crash, cabin objects cause mechanical injuries; the force may be a hundred, even a thousand times greater than in other transport trauma. In a pilot, the head strikes the panel, the palm is squeezed between the control wheel and the panel, and the foot strikes the control pedals. Prints of the pedal may be found on the sole of the footwear, and of the relief of the control wheel on the glove. From the action of the harness, an arc-shaped abrasion, a bruise, a transverse rupture of the abdominal wall, and sometimes separation of the upper part of the trunk are observed on the abdomen and chest.

t: Aviation trauma: explosion, thermal and toxic action
n: Explosion, thermal and toxic action in aviation trauma. On impact with the ground, fuel tanks may explode; the blast wave destroys the body, and fragments are scattered in a radius of up to 500 m. In a fire, clothing ignites and the body burns, sometimes to charring. Because the tanks are in the middle of the fuselage, passengers have more thermal injuries. When paints and polymer materials burn, carbon monoxide, formaldehyde and vinyl chloride are formed; engine gases and fuel vapour also poison. The edge of a wing, propeller blades and jet engine gas cause injury at 500-600 degrees. The pilot's body is examined thoroughly.

t: Case analysis: rail and aviation trauma
n: Case analysis: rail and aviation trauma. First situation: a victim beside a railway has a T-shaped abrasion on the side facing the wheel, and oil and coal particles have been found on the clothing. These signs are characteristic of rail trauma. The pressure band on the body is at first soft and whitish, and on drying becomes coarse and dark brown. Second situation: in the body from an air crash, the eardrum is ruptured and there are haemorrhages in the middle and inner ear cavities. Question: what is the cause of the disaster in the second case? Answer: these signs indicate failure of cabin pressurisation, that is, explosive decompression.

t: Conclusions and review questions
n: Conclusion. Transport trauma is the totality of injuries received from parts of a moving vehicle and in a fall from it. More than 90% of examinations are car trauma. The physician fully describes the injury; removes clothing and footwear carefully, dries them if necessary, wraps them in paper and hands them to law enforcement. The expert establishes the type of trauma, the mechanism and the victim's position, and analysis of examination materials gives recommendations for reducing traumatism. Review questions: types of bumper injuries, formation of pressure and sliding bands in rail trauma, injuring factors in aviation trauma.
